images.text:
Vanessa: Ummm. This coffee is good.
Amy: Yes, and this dessert is delicious too. Peter what are you doing?
Peter: That bite of your cake was so amazing that I decided to get one of my own.
Amy: So, Vanessa. It's your turn to tell a story. I want to know how you became a manager at Bistro 88.

Vanessa: Sure. When I first came in, Bill Williams was running the place. Did you ever meet Bill, Peter?
Peter: No, I never met Bill.
Vanessa: Bill had made a lot of money on the stockmarket. He made so much money that he decided to open his own restaurant. The problem was, Bill and his partners didn't know anything about running a restaurant. He lacked the insight and the tenacity needed to make things work in the restaurant business.
Peter: Was he a nice guy?

Vanessa: Oh he was a great guy, but he didn't know how to organize employees and he didn't know what to give customers. At one point, he created such turmoil that half of his staff quit on him. When I first walked into the kitchen, several people were busily cooking, some were preparing food, some weren't doing anything, the chef was yelling, and the customers were waiting to be helped. One customer was yelling at a server and waving his hands. Others were complaining to each other about the bad service. Soon after that, it was such a disorganized mess that most of the chefs quit and because I was still there I got promoted to head chef. After a month, Bill confided in me that he didn't want to run the place anymore. He just wanted to own it and asked me if I wanted to manage it and I said yes.
Amy: You were able to turn things around that quickly?
Vanessa: No, we treaded water for about six months while I implemented my vision for the place. Bill was willing to spend some money so that we could hire some hot young chefs. We got a few good reviews and through social media and a lot of hard work, we were able to get the word out.
Peter: Huh? I never knew that. So are we going to play some games?

Cause and Effect: So/Such ... That + Clause
When you want to talk about a remarkable situation (one that is extraordinary or unusual), you can use the structure So/Such ... That + Clause.

So and such are degree intensifiers (emphasizers) that combine with other modifiers to express a remarkable situation, which is followed by that + clause that expresses an effect.

For example:
They earned so much money that they could go on a trip around the world.

The cause is: They earned a lot of money.
The effect is: They could go on a trip around the world.

You use such before an adjective + noun.

For example:
Doctors are such nice people.
That bite of your cake was so amazing that I decided to get one of my own.
Bill was willing to spend some money so that we could hire some hot young chefs.
He made so much money that he decided to open his own restaurant.
He created such turmoil that half of his staff quit on him.
It was such a disorganized mess that most of the chefs quit.
The Past Continuous vs. The Simple Past
You use the Simple Past in a narrative to talk about a single, complete past event. You use the Past Continuous tense to talk about the background situation that existed at the time.

For example:
Mike dropped his wallet while he was getting into the taxi.
She was shaking with fear as she left the party.

The one-time event might have interrupted the situation, or have happened while the situation was in progress.
